intro: The Tanakh has three parts: Torah, Nevi'im and Ketuvim. You have read the Torah and the history books that follow it. This unit covers everything else: the books of the prophets who spoke to kings and crowds, and the Writings, the most varied shelf in the Bible, with songs, sayings, a debate about suffering, love poems, court tales and the story of the return from exile.

These books matter because they are the ones Jewish communities hear most often outside the Torah itself. A passage from the Prophets is chanted every Shabbat as the haftarah. The Psalms fill the prayer book. Five short scrolls mark five holidays. Knowing these books means knowing what a Jewish year sounds like, and it means meeting texts that Christians also read, sometimes in different ways.

By the end of this unit you will be able to explain what a prophet does and how a prophetic book is built, name the main prophets and what each said, describe how a psalm works, tell the three wisdom books apart, match each of the five scrolls to its holiday, and explain why the Tanakh ends with a call to go up to Jerusalem. You will do this by reading passages closely and by noticing how different readers have understood them.
bigQuestion: What did the prophets and the Writings say to their first readers, and how do Jewish communities still hear them through the year?

timeline.t: Amos speaks against injustice in the northern kingdom
Isaiah of Jerusalem begins to speak during the Assyrian threat
Assyria takes Samaria; the northern kingdom ends
Sennacherib besieges Jerusalem; Isaiah tells Hezekiah the city will stand
Jeremiah is called in the days of King Josiah
Ezekiel's visions begin among the exiles in Babylonia
Babylon burns Jerusalem and the Temple; Lamentations mourns the city
Cyrus of Persia lets the exiles return
Nehemiah rebuilds the walls; Ezra reads the Torah at the Water Gate
Many scholars date the final form of Daniel to the Maccabean revolt
The haftarah, the Psalms and the five scrolls are read through the Jewish year

words.d: the Hebrew word for prophet; a messenger who speaks for God
a prophetic message, often in poetry, to a nation, king or city
an action a prophet performs with his own body to act out a message
the reading from the Prophets that follows the Torah reading on Shabbat and holidays
"the Twelve," the twelve short prophetic books counted as one book
forced removal from one's land; Judah's exile in Babylon began in 597 and 586 BCE
the Writings, the third part of the Tanakh
the pattern of Hebrew poetry in which the second half of a line echoes or contrasts with the first
books that teach how to live: Proverbs, Job and Ecclesiastes
the five scrolls, each read on a holiday: Song of Songs, Ruth, Lamentations, Ecclesiastes, Esther
a language related to Hebrew used in the Persian empire; parts of Daniel and Ezra are in it
"going up": to Jerusalem, to the Torah reading, or to live in the land of Israel

test.q: In the Tanakh, what is a prophet mainly?
choices: A messenger who delivers God's words to people
A fortune teller who predicts the future for pay
A priest who runs the Temple
test.why: The Hebrew navi is a messenger; the books open speeches with "Thus saith the LORD."

test.q: Which books belong to the Latter Prophets?
choices: Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel and the Twelve
test.why: The Latter Prophets are the books of speeches; Joshua through Kings are the Former Prophets.

choices: A sign-act telling Judah to bear Babylon's rule rather than rebel
A tool for plowing his field at Anathoth
test.why: Jeremiah 27–28 describes the wooden yoke as a sign-act; Hananiah broke it.

test.q: How do the JPS 1917 and King James translations differ at Isaiah 7:14?
test.why: The Hebrew word is almah; JPS reads "young woman" and the KJV "virgin," and the two traditions read the sign differently.

test.q: Why do many scholars think Isaiah 40–66 was written during or after the exile?
choices: It names Cyrus and speaks to exiles in Babylon
test.why: Cyrus (Isaiah 45:1) ruled about 150 years after Isaiah of Jerusalem; Jewish tradition read the book as one.

test.q: What does Ezekiel 37 say the dry bones represent?
test.why: Ezekiel 37:11 explains that the bones are the house of Israel, whose hope seems lost.

test.q: Which verse names doing justly, loving mercy and walking humbly with God?
test.why: Micah 6:8 sums up what God requires in those three actions; Amos 5:24 is justice like water.

test.q: Why is Jonah read on Yom Kippur afternoon?
choices: Because Jonah was a high priest
Because it is set in Jerusalem
Because it lists the day's sacrifices
Because it shows that even Israel's enemies can repent and be forgiven
test.why: Jewish tradition reads Jonah as a lesson in repentance and God's mercy toward Nineveh.

test.q: How is the book of Psalms divided?
choices: Into five books, each ending with a blessing
Into twelve books for the tribes
Into two books, David's and Solomon's
test.why: Psalms has 150 poems in five books; the midrash compared them to the five books of the Torah.

test.q: Which type of psalm cries for help and usually ends by turning to trust?
test.why: Laments, such as Psalm 13 and Psalm 22, are the largest group in the book.

test.q: What does Koheleth mean by hevel, translated "vanity" in JPS 1917?
choices: Breath or vapor, something that passes
test.why: Hevel is breath; Ecclesiastes uses it to say that everything under the sun passes.

test.q: Which scroll is read on Tisha B'Av?
test.why: Lamentations mourns the fall of Jerusalem and is chanted on the fast of the ninth of Av.

test.q: Why is Ruth read at Shavuot, according to tradition?
choices: Its harvest setting, Ruth's choice of the Torah and her descendant David
Because it takes place in Babylon
test.why: Tradition gives those reasons: the barley harvest, Ruth's joining the people, and David's birth on Shavuot.

test.q: How does the Talmud (Yoma 9b) describe what happened after Haggai, Zechariah and Malachi?
choices: The spirit of prophecy departed from Israel
test.why: The Talmud teaches that prophecy ended with those three, and guidance came through study of the text.

test.q: How does the book of Chronicles, last in the traditional order of the Tanakh, end?
choices: With Cyrus's decree that the people may go up to Jerusalem
With the destruction of the Temple
test.why: 2 Chronicles 36:23 repeats Cyrus's decree and ends with "let him go up," the root of the word aliyah.

write.prompt: Do the prophets and the Writings agree about how the world works? Choose two or three passages from this unit (for example Amos 5:24, Micah 6:8, Job 38:4 or Ecclesiastes 9:11) and explain what each says. Then show how two readers, such as Rashi, the Talmud, a modern scholar or a Christian reader, have understood one of them. End with what the passages together suggest and what they leave open.
tips: Name the book, chapter and verse of every passage you cite, and the translation you read it in.
Attribute every belief: say "Jewish tradition teaches" or "Rashi reads" or "many scholars think," not "it is true that."
Compare readings; do not judge which tradition is right.
Use the unit's terms, such as oracle, parallelism, haftarah and Megillot, and explain each one the first time.
Keep sentences short and say one idea at a time.
